Question 3A (2 marks). Recall that if `s` is a variable then `${s:offset:len}` expands to the substring of `s` starting at index `offset` and having length `len`.

Using one or two lines of Bash, how could you print the first half of a string stored in a variable `s`? Assume that the string has even length.
questions.grading: `${#s}` gives the length; integer division by 2; then `${s:0:n}` (`$n` inside is also fine). One-liner `echo "${s:0:${#s}/2}"` is correct too. Common mistakes: `$s.length`, `${s:0:${#s/2}}`, or using `expr` incorrectly.

rubric.item: Computes half the length with `${#s}` and arithmetic `/ 2`
Prints `${s:0:n}` (substring from index 0 of length n)

questions.prompt:
Question 3B (2 marks). Suppose that you have a file named `classlist` that contains the last name, first name, and
student number of each student in a course. A tab character separates the last name from the first
name and the first name from the student number. For example:

```
Cade	Barry	3100025
Day	Holly	2999999
Friese	Andy	3001111
Yu	Sue	1990000
```

Write a single pipeline that extracts the student numbers from the file `classlist`, sorts the student numbers in ascending order, saves all the student numbers to a file named `snum` (in sorted order), and prints the first three student numbers (in sorted order). Hint: You need a `tee` somewhere in the pipeline.
questions.answer:
```bash
cut -f3 classlist | sort | tee snum | head -n 3
```
questions.grading: `cut -f3` (tab is cut's default delimiter; `-d $'\t'` is fine). `sort` or `sort -n` both fine (all numbers have 7 digits). `tee snum` must come AFTER sort and BEFORE head, otherwise snum is unsorted or only has 3 lines. `head -3` is accepted. `cut -d ' '` is wrong (fields are tab-separated).

rubric.item: `cut -f3 classlist | sort` extracts and sorts the student numbers
`tee snum` placed after sort and before `head -n 3`

questions.prompt:
Question 3B (2 marks). Suppose that you have a file named `classlist` that contains the last name, first name, and
student number of each student in a course. A tab character separates the last name from the first
name and the first name from the student number. For example:

```
Cade	Barry	3100025
Day	Holly	2999999
Friese	Andy	3001111
Yu	Sue	1990000
```

Write a single pipeline that extracts the last names from the file `classlist`, sorts them in reverse (descending) alphabetical order, saves all the sorted last names to a file named `lastnames`, and prints the first two last names (in that sorted order). Hint: You need a `tee` somewhere in the pipeline.
questions.answer:
```bash
cut -f1 classlist | sort -r | tee lastnames | head -n 2
```
questions.grading: Needs field 1, `sort -r`, `tee lastnames` between sort and head, and `head -n 2` (or `head -2`). For the sample file the output is `Yu` then `Friese`. Putting tee before sort, or after head, loses the second mark.

questions.prompt:
Question 4 (4 marks).

Write a script that accepts two command line arguments that are both file names. The first
argument is the name of the source file, and the second argument is the name of the destination
file.

The script sets the permissions of the destination file to be equal to the permissions of the source
file (i.e., it copies the permissions from the source file to the destination file).

No error checking is required in this question. You can assume that two command line
arguments are always given, and that the source and destination files exist.

From Assignment 2 recall that the `stat` command can print the permissions of a file:

```bash
stat -c %a filename
```

prints the three-digit octal permissions of the file named `filename`.
questions.answer:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

src=$1
dest=$2

# permissions of src
perm=$(stat -c %a "$src")

chmod "$perm" "$dest"
```
questions.grading: Essential: command substitution `$(stat -c %a "$src")` and `chmod` with that value on the destination. The posted solution says the quotes around `"$src"` and `"$dest"` are REQUIRED (file names may contain spaces): unquoted filename expansions lose a mark. Quoting `$perm` is optional. A one-liner `chmod "$(stat -c %a "$1")" "$2"` is full marks. `chmod --reference="$1" "$2"` works on Linux but ignores the hint; accept it. Backticks instead of `$( )` are fine. Getting source/destination backwards loses 1 mark.

rubric.item: `#!/bin/bash` and uses `$1` as source, `$2` as destination
`chmod` applies those permissions to the destination

questions.prompt:
Question 4 (4 marks).

Write a script that accepts two command line arguments that are both file names. The first
argument is the name of the destination file, and the second argument is the name of the source
(reference) file.

The script prints the message `setting permissions of DEST to PERM` (where DEST is the destination
file name and PERM is the three-digit octal permissions of the source file), and then sets the permissions
of the destination file to be equal to the permissions of the source file.

No error checking is required in this question. You can assume that two command line
arguments are always given, and that the source and destination files exist.

From Assignment 2 recall that the `stat` command can print the permissions of a file:

```bash
stat -c %a filename
```

prints the three-digit octal permissions of the file named `filename`.
questions.answer:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

dest=$1
src=$2

perm=$(stat -c %a "$src")
echo "setting permissions of $dest to $perm"
chmod "$perm" "$dest"
```
questions.grading: Note the argument ORDER is reversed from the usual: `$1` is the destination. Must stat the source (`$2`). Quotes on filename variables required. The message must use the destination name and the octal permissions.

rubric.item: `#!/bin/bash`, `$1` used as destination and `$2` as source
Prints the required message and runs `chmod "$perm" "$dest"`

questions.prompt:
Question 5 (10 marks).

The fact that file removal in Linux is permanent can be inconvenient. Instead of removing a file,
we can create a command that moves the file into a hidden trashcan directory.

Create a script named `trash.sh` that moves a single file into a hidden trashcan directory by
performing the following steps:

1. finds the name of the directory `dir` that the file is located in
2. creates a directory named `.trash` in `dir`
3. changes the permissions of the `.trash` directory so that the owner has all permissions
   and all other users have no permissions
4. prints the message `"moving filename to the trashcan"` where `filename` is the
   first command line argument provided to the script (see below)
5. moves the file into the `.trash` directory created in Step 2

Obviously, the script requires one command line argument (the pathname of the file to move into
the trash).

No error checking is required. Assume that one command line argument is always provided to
the script, and that the argument is the pathname to a file that is owned by the user of the script.
Also, assume that the pathname always includes the directory that the file is located in.

Step 2 will cause an error message to be printed if the directory `.trash` already exists in `dir`.
You should ignore the fact that this error can occur.

Hint: If `str` is a variable then `${str%pattern}` expands to the string formed by removing the
shortest trailing part of `str` that matches `pattern`.

Example 1:
```
trash.sh ./myfile
```
moves `./myfile` into the `.trash` directory created in the current working directory

Example 2:
```
trash.sh /home/user1/somedir/myfile
```
moves `/home/user1/somedir/myfile` into the `.trash` directory created in the directory
`/home/user1/somedir/`
questions.answer:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

pathname=$1

# Step 1
dir=${pathname%/*}

# Step 2
trashdir=$dir/.trash
mkdir "$trashdir"

# Step 3
chmod u=rwx,go= "$trashdir"     # or: chmod 700 "$trashdir"

# Step 4
echo "moving $pathname to the trashcan"

# Step 5
mv "$pathname" "$trashdir"
```
questions.grading: Step 1: `${pathname%/*}` removes the shortest trailing `/name`, leaving the directory (`dirname "$1"` is also accepted). Step 3: `chmod 700` or `chmod u=rwx,go=` (`chmod go-rwx` alone is not enough unless u=rwx is also set). Quotes are required around pathname variables in `mkdir`, `chmod` and `mv`; missing quotes lose marks. NOTE: the posted 2023 solution writes `mv "$pathname $trashdir"`, which is a typo (it makes one argument); the correct form is `mv "$pathname" "$trashdir"`. Using `rm` or `cp` instead of `mv` in step 5 loses that step. Using `##` instead of `%` in step 1 gives the filename, not the directory (wrong).

questions.prompt:
Question 5 (10 marks).

Before editing a file it can be useful to keep a backup copy. Create a script named `backup.sh` that copies a
single file into a hidden backup directory by performing the following steps:

1. finds the name of the directory `dir` that the file is located in, and the name `name` of the file itself
   (the pathname without its directory part)
2. creates a directory named `.backup` in `dir`
3. changes the permissions of the `.backup` directory so that the owner has all permissions, the group has
   read and execute permissions, and all other users have no permissions
4. prints the message `"backing up filename"` where `filename` is the first command line argument provided to
   the script
5. copies the file into the `.backup` directory created in Step 2, naming the copy `name.bak` (e.g., a file
   `notes.txt` is copied to `.backup/notes.txt.bak`)

The script requires one command line argument (the pathname of the file to back up).

No error checking is required. Assume that one command line argument is always provided, that it is the
pathname of a file owned by the user, and that the pathname always includes the directory that the file is
located in. Step 2 prints an error if `.backup` already exists; ignore this.

Hint: If `str` is a variable then `${str%pattern}` removes the shortest trailing part of `str` matching
`pattern`, and `${str##pattern}` removes the longest leading part of `str` matching `pattern`.

Example:
```
backup.sh /home/user1/somedir/notes.txt
```
creates `/home/user1/somedir/.backup` and copies the file to `/home/user1/somedir/.backup/notes.txt.bak`
questions.answer:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

pathname=$1

# Step 1
dir=${pathname%/*}
name=${pathname##*/}

# Step 2
backupdir=$dir/.backup
mkdir "$backupdir"

# Step 3
chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o= "$backupdir"     # or: chmod 750 "$backupdir"

# Step 4
echo "backing up $pathname"

# Step 5
cp "$pathname" "$backupdir/$name.bak"
```
questions.grading: `${pathname##*/}` gives the file name (longest leading `*/` removed); `basename "$1"` accepted. Permissions must be 750 (`u=rwx,g=rx,o=`). Copy, not move. All pathname variables must be quoted (names may contain spaces). The `.bak` suffix must be appended to the name: `"$backupdir/$name.bak"`.

rubric.item: Step 1: dir via `${pathname%/*}` and name via `${pathname##*/}`
